s: Which one of the following sites is associated with joint or double burial in the Harappan context?
x: Lothal is associated with joint or double burial. Ropar is noted for a dog buried with a human, while Surkotada is associated with pot burials.
tq: Use the site-specific association and distinguish closely related burial practices.
sec: Burial practices → site (extended, pot, joint/double, fractional; R-37, Cemetery-H, Sanauli, Lothal, Kalibangan)

s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Surkotada — Pot burial
2. Ropar — Dog buried with a human
3. Lothal — Joint or double burial
4. Harappa Cemetery-H — Post-cremation burial
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
x: All four pairs are correctly matched. Surkotada had pot burials, Ropar had dog-human burial, Lothal had joint burial, and Cemetery-H at Harappa had post-cremation burial.
tq: Check each site against its distinctive burial feature before selecting the coded combination.
sec: Burial practices → site (extended, pot, joint/double, fractional; R-37, Cemetery-H, Sanauli, Lothal, Kalibangan)

s: Which one of the following best describes fractional burial at Mohenjodaro and Harappa?
o: Ashes were placed in a pottery urn after cremation
Bones were buried after exposure of the body
The complete body was buried with a coffin
A human was buried together with a dog
x: Fractional burial involved burying bones after the body had been exposed. Complete coffin burial, post-cremation burial and dog-human burial represent different practices.
tq: Discriminate between similar burial categories by identifying the treatment of the body or bones.
sec: Burial practices → site (extended, pot, joint/double, fractional; R-37, Cemetery-H, Sanauli, Lothal, Kalibangan)

s:

Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements are correct. Extended burials occurred at Mohenjodaro and Harappa, Cemetery-H had post-cremation burials, and Ropar had dog-human burials in oval pits.
tq: Verify the site and burial form in each statement; the combination includes three independently established facts.
sec: Burial practices → site (extended, pot, joint/double, fractional; R-37, Cemetery-H, Sanauli, Lothal, Kalibangan)

o: They followed a standard east-west orientation and contained no pottery.
They followed a standard north-south orientation and included pots of provisions.
They consisted of joint burials with dogs in oval pits.
They were exclusively post-cremation burials in Cemetery-H.

s: The presence of pottery, ornaments, mirrors, beads and food in graves is generally interpreted as evidence of:

s: Which of the following is the strongest material indicator of social differentiation in Harappan society?
o: The absence of written royal genealogies
The existence of only one type of house
Variation in burial goods and ornament quality
x: Differences in the quantity and quality of burial goods and ornaments suggest differentiation in social status. Uniformity in bricks is evidence mainly relevant to organisation and authority.
tq: Identify the material evidence that directly reflects unequal status rather than administrative standardisation.
sec: Social stratification evidence - house sizes, citadel vs lower town, burial goods

s:
Consider the following statements regarding settlement layout and social stratification in the Harappan civilisation:
1. The citadel was generally situated to the west.
2. The lower town was generally situated to the east.
3. Public buildings and elite areas were associated with the citadel.
4. The lower town contained houses of commoners.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All four statements are correct. The western citadel contained public and elite areas, while the eastern lower town was associated with commoners' houses.
tq: Check the directional, functional and social attributes of the two settlement zones.
sec: Social stratification evidence - house sizes, citadel vs lower town, burial goods

s: Which one of the following was NOT identified as a category of Harappan building?
x: The three broad building types mentioned are residential buildings, larger buildings and public buildings. No royal palace has been identified.
tq: Find the option that contradicts the documented building classification and palace evidence.
sec: Social stratification evidence - house sizes, citadel vs lower town, burial goods

s: Single-roomed barracks have been reported particularly at:
x: Single-roomed barracks are reported at Harappa and form part of the evidence for variation in building types and living arrangements.
tq: Recall the site attached to the distinctive single-roomed barracks.
sec: Social stratification evidence - house sizes, citadel vs lower town, burial goods

s: Which statement best reflects the scholarly position on the alleged four-fold division of Harappan society into scholars, warriors, traders and labourers?
o: It is directly confirmed by Harappan inscriptions.
It is explicitly described in royal genealogies.
It is identical to the Later Vedic caste system.
It is a speculative interpretation based on material evidence.
x: The four-fold division into scholars, warriors, traders and labourers is speculative. There is no textual evidence establishing it as a rigid social order.
tq: Distinguish a cautious scholarly inference from a directly documented institution.
sec: Social stratification evidence - house sizes, citadel vs lower town, burial goods

s: Which of the following statements regarding caste in the Harappan civilisation is correct?
o: A rigid caste system is clearly described in Harappan texts.
Caste crystallised only in the Later Vedic period, and no textual evidence proves a rigid Harappan caste system.
The Harappan script gives the names of four caste groups.
Caste was absent from the Later Vedic period but present in Harappan cities.
x: There is no textual evidence for a rigid caste system in the Harappan civilisation; caste is considered to have crystallised in the Later Vedic period.
tq: Separate Harappan material-based inferences from the later textual development of caste.
sec: Social stratification evidence - house sizes, citadel vs lower town, burial goods

s: Female skeletons recovered at Rakhigarhi were found wearing:

x: Female skeletons at Rakhigarhi were found with jasper and agate beads and shell bangles.
tq: Use the specific combination of materials to identify the correct archaeological observation.

s: Which one of the following views is associated with the interpretation of Harappan polity as a priestly rule?
o: The exclusive presence of horse-drawn chariots
The presence of citadels, the Great Bath and the steatite Priest-King
The use of hereditary Vedic assemblies
The absence of all public structures
x: The priest-rule interpretation draws on the citadel, Great Bath and steatite Priest-King. These features have also been interpreted in other ways and do not conclusively prove priestly rule.
tq: Match a political interpretation with the evidence used to support it.
sec: Polity debate - priest rule, merchant class, city-state vs centralised state

s: The interpretation of Harappan polity as being dominated by merchant elites or civic administrators is based chiefly on:
o: The discovery of numerous royal inscriptions
Trade-driven uniformity and the absence of clear kings or palaces
The existence of hereditary monarchy in every city
The presence of large standing armies
x: Trade-driven uniformity, together with the absence of identifiable kings and palaces, has been used to argue for merchant elites or civic administrators.
tq: Link each political model to the evidence cited for it rather than to an unrelated feature.
sec: Polity debate - priest rule, merchant class, city-state vs centralised state

s:
Consider the following pairs:

2. Planned cities and advanced drainage — Municipal governance
3. Trade-driven uniformity — Merchant elites or civic administrators
4. Great Bath and Priest-King — Priest-rule interpretation
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
x: All four pairs are correctly matched with the interpretations used in the debate over Harappan political organisation.

sec: Polity debate - priest rule, merchant class, city-state vs centralised state

s: Which statement most accurately describes the present understanding of Harappan political structure?
o: There is no clear-cut evidence, and the polity appears corporate.
It is conclusively known to have been a priestly theocracy.
It is conclusively known to have been a hereditary monarchy.
Every city was governed directly from a single identified capital.
x: The political structure is not clear-cut and has been described as appearing corporate. The evidence does not conclusively establish a monarchy, priestly theocracy or single capital.
tq: Prefer the carefully qualified interpretation over absolute political labels unsupported by evidence.
sec: Polity debate - priest rule, merchant class, city-state vs centralised state

s: The centralised-state argument for the Harappan civilisation relies mainly on:
o: Uniformity over a very large geographical area
The discovery of one undisputed royal capital
The names of rulers in the Harappan script
The presence of temples in every settlement
x: The centralised-state argument is based chiefly on the striking uniformity spread over a very large area. No single capital or ruler has been conclusively identified.
tq: Identify the principal evidence used by one side of a historical debate.
sec: Polity debate - priest rule, merchant class, city-state vs centralised state

s: Which observation is most consistent with the city-state interpretation of Harappan polity?
o: The script records a succession of kings.
All settlements were governed from a palace at Harappa.
Uniform bricks prove the existence of a hereditary emperor.
Several large cities existed, but no single capital has been identified.
x: The city-state argument points to the existence of several large cities without a clearly identified single capital.
tq: Apply the distinction between a centralised state and multiple city-centred polities.

Lothal — Iron weapons; Chanhudaro — Royal palaces
Lothal — Horse breeding; Chanhudaro — Vedic schools
Lothal — Temple sculpture; Chanhudaro — Coin minting

s: Which one of the following statements about Harappan monumental architecture is NOT correct?
o: Harappan cities possessed great palaces and temples as a general rule.
No royal palaces have been found.
The Great Bath and other public structures have been identified.

s: The absence of monumental temples and palaces in Harappan cities has been interpreted as possibly indicating that:
o: The Great Bath was a royal palace
Religion and political authority were completely absent
Worship may have been domestic or open-air and power was not personalised in a king
Every settlement was controlled by a foreign emperor
x: One interpretation is that worship occurred in domestic or open-air settings and that political power was not personalised in a king. Public structures were chiefly civic in character.
tq: Connect an archaeological absence with the cautious interpretations proposed for it.

s: Which of the following was regarded as a civic public structure rather than a royal palace or monumental temple?
x: The Great Bath, along with structures such as granaries and pillared halls, is interpreted as a civic public structure.

s:
